title: Cerebellar Learning in Action

The preceding subsections separated cerebellar learning into three analytically distinct components: the loss that specifies what should be predicted or corrected, the neural error signal that represents the remaining mismatch, and the plasticity that changes the circuit responsible for it. In the behaving cerebellum, however, these are not separate stages. They are three descriptions of one continuously running calibration process. A mismatch between predicted and actual consequence is a loss when viewed from outside the circuit; it becomes an error signal when encoded by the olivocerebellar and related feedback pathways; and it becomes learning when that signal modifies the recent activity responsible for the prediction.

The continuously running calibration cycle

On each cycle, mossy fibers provide the current sensory state, efference copy, task context, and recent history; the granule-cell layer expands these inputs into a high-dimensional temporal basis; and learned Purkinje-cell and nuclear activity generates a prediction or anticipatory correction. The actual sensory, motor, or internal consequence then arrives. Any residual mismatch is routed back through the climbing-fiber system or other task-relevant teaching pathways, while eligibility traces identify the parallel-fiber and local circuit activity that preceded it. Plasticity across the cerebellar cortex and nuclei alters the next output produced from the same context, so that the prediction occurs earlier, with a more appropriate timing and gain, and the subsequent residual becomes smaller 1, 2, 3. Granule and climbing-fiber signals can be imaged together (Figure) 107. Cerebellar input activity changes with learned reward timing (Figure).

Learning therefore converts delayed correction into anticipatory control. Early in training, an unexpected consequence strongly recruits the teaching system and behavior depends heavily on reactive feedback. With repetition, predictable structure is absorbed into Purkinje-cell and nuclear output, allowing the correction to begin before the delayed consequence arrives. At convergence, the teaching signal need not disappear entirely; rather, its component predictable from the preceding context should be reduced or decorrelated from the parallel-fiber basis that once predicted it 4. When an expected consequence is omitted, the residual can reverse direction and train extinction or an opposing calibration 5.

This update is distributed rather than localized to a single synapse. Parallel-fiber–Purkinje plasticity changes the learned cortical output; inhibitory, granular-layer, and intrinsic plasticity reshape its timing, representation, and gain; and plasticity in the cerebellar and vestibular nuclei changes how Purkinje inhibition is combined with excitatory afferent input to produce the final correction 3. The resulting memory is therefore not simply a stored movement but a context-indexed change in how the circuit predicts a future event and prepares the rest of the nervous system for it 6.

The completeness of this transduction chain varies across experimental paradigms. In eyeblink conditioning and saccade adaptation, individual links from the teaching event to Purkinje-cell change and subsequent behavior have been demonstrated directly 7, 8. In vestibulo-ocular, reaching, locomotor, and speech adaptation, the objective and cerebellum-dependent behavioral update are well established, but parts of the cellular chain remain inferred or differ across training conditions. Proposed cognitive and affective applications are less complete still: cerebellar prediction-error activity and causal behavioral contributions are increasingly evident, while the corresponding local targets, climbing-fiber signals, and plasticity rules remain unresolved. The following case studies should therefore be read both as demonstrations of a common predictive-calibration architecture and as a progression from circuits whose learning rules are understood in considerable detail to domains in which the same computational interpretation remains provisional. Recent human fMRI evidence extends cerebellar prediction-error learning to passive, nonmotor statistical learning (Figure) 106. Recent human fMRI evidence extends cerebellar prediction-error learning to passive, nonmotor statistical learning (Figure).

Vestibulo-ocular-reflex adaptation

The vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) is the cleanest systems-level example of cerebellar predictive calibration. When the head turns, vestibular pathways drive the eyes in the opposite direction, stabilizing the image on the retina before visual feedback could generate a sufficiently rapid correction. If the eye movement has the wrong gain or phase, however, the visual scene moves across the retina as retinal slip. Experiments induce adaptation by repeatedly pairing head motion with visual motion that makes the normal reflex too weak, too strong, or incorrectly phased. Over training, the VOR changes accordingly; when subsequently measured in darkness, the adapted response persists despite the absence of visual feedback, showing that the mismatch has been converted into a learned feedforward command rather than merely corrected online 9, 10.

The transduction chain begins with vestibular mossy-fiber signals that represent head motion and provide related input to both the floccular cortex and vestibular nuclei. Purkinje-cell simple spikes supply a learned inhibitory signal to the vestibular nuclei, where it is combined with direct vestibular input to determine compensatory eye velocity. Retinal slip recruits visual climbing-fiber signals from the inferior olive whose phase relative to head motion specifies the direction in which the reflex should change. Parallel-fiber activity representing the preceding vestibular state is thereby associated with the later visual consequence, and altered Purkinje output changes the gain and phase of the next eye movement. The same retinal slip is therefore simultaneously the behavioral loss, the source of the teaching signal, and the event that assigns credit to the preceding sensorimotor context 9, 11.

No single synaptic rule, however, accounts for the complete learned response. Selectively blocking PKC-dependent LTD in Purkinje cells leaves the baseline reflex largely intact but abolishes adaptation during short visual–vestibular training, demonstrating that the normal circuit can execute the reflex while being unable to recalibrate it 10. Conversely, deleting PP2B from Purkinje cells abolishes postsynaptic potentiation and impairs both gain-increase and gain-decrease adaptation, showing that bidirectional changes are needed to move the controller in opposite directions and prevent its weights from saturating 12. Yet LTD-deficient mice recover partial adaptation over many days, indicating that slower plasticity elsewhere in the circuit can compensate for loss of the canonical cortical rule 13.

The memory is correspondingly distributed across cell types and timescales. VOR learning changes the phase of molecular-layer-interneuron activity, and suppressing these interneurons after gain-increase training abolishes expression of the newly acquired response without disrupting the baseline reflex 14; after several days of consolidation, however, the same suppression no longer removes the memory. Longer or spaced training also produces adaptations that become less sensitive to temporary floccular inactivation, consistent with increasing storage or expression in vestibular nuclear pathways 15. This should not be described as an obligatory transfer from one exclusive storage site to another: cortical and nuclear plasticity interact, and the apparent locus of the memory depends on the form and duration of training 11. Eyeblink conditioning produces a learned anticipatory response (Figure) 108. A 2025 mouse study tests climbing fibers during oculomotor learning (Figure) 117. The study also tests inhibition after acquisition (Figure).

Even the climbing-fiber teacher is less obligatory than the simplest Marr–Albus–Ito account predicts. Rhesus monkeys can show robust VOR adaptation under specially designed conditions that evoke little or no normal climbing-fiber modulation; in those conditions, Purkinje simple-spike activity still predicts the direction and magnitude of learning. Climbing fibers and simple spikes may therefore provide partially substitutable or additive instructive signals, depending on the statistics of the task 9. The VOR remains the clearest example of the general calibration loop, but precisely because it reveals both sides of the principle: repeated retinal error is transformed into an anticipatory correction, while the biological implementation distributes that transformation across multiple signals and plasticity sites rather than relying on a single universal update rule. Experimental results distinguish candidate teaching signals (Figure).

Eyeblink conditioning

Delay eyeblink conditioning isolates the temporal core of cerebellar learning. A neutral conditioned stimulus, such as a tone or light, is repeatedly followed after a fixed interval by an air puff or periocular stimulus that reflexively closes the eyelid. With training, the conditioned stimulus comes to evoke a blink whose maximum closure occurs immediately before the expected unconditioned stimulus. The learned response is therefore not merely an association between two events: it is a prediction of both what will occur and when it will occur 16, 7.

The full transduction chain is unusually explicit. Information about the conditioned stimulus reaches the cerebellum through mossy-fiber pathways and is expanded into a temporally evolving granule-cell representation. The unconditioned stimulus activates climbing fibers from the inferior olive, producing complex spikes that instruct plasticity in the preceding context. Over repeated pairings, Purkinje cells in the eyelid-controlling region acquire a precisely timed pause in simple-spike firing. This pause releases the anterior interposed nucleus from inhibition, allowing nuclear output to drive eyelid closure before the air puff arrives. Plasticity in the nuclei also contributes, so the conditioned response is produced by an interacting cortical–nuclear memory rather than by one modified synapse alone 17, 18, 19. Climbing-fiber stimulation can instruct eyeblink conditioning (Figure).

Recent causal experiments establish the climbing-fiber event as an instructive signal rather than a correlate of the aversive stimulus or reflex blink. Optogenetic climbing-fiber activation could replace the air puff and train a conditioned response even when the stimulation itself produced no reflexive blink; changing the interval between the conditioned stimulus and climbing-fiber activation shifted the timing of the learned response accordingly. Conversely, temporally selective suppression of the natural climbing-fiber response blocked learning. The circuit is therefore trained by the complex-spike event itself, not by observing the corrective eyelid movement that normally accompanies the unconditioned stimulus 7.

The resulting Purkinje-cell output contains the learned interval. Recordings during conditioning show that the conditioned simple-spike pause develops gradually and that its onset, maximum, and offset shift when the interval between the conditioned and unconditioned stimuli is changed. The pause is thus not a generic command to blink after hearing a tone; it is a temporally shaped prediction whose profile places the nuclear disinhibition near the expected arrival of the teaching event 16, 20.

Learning also changes the teaching signal itself. Climbing fibers respond strongly when the air puff is unexpected, develop responses to cues that predict it, and signal its unexpected omission, resembling a temporally structured prediction error rather than a fixed sensory relay 21. During extinction, presenting the conditioned stimulus without the expected air puff transiently suppresses olivary activity below baseline (a marker of learned Purkinje inhibition without matching olivary excitation); blocking this inhibition prevents extinction, whereas selective activation of GABAergic nucleo-olivary input is sufficient to extinguish the learned blink even when normal paired trials continue 22, 5.

Eyeblink conditioning therefore displays the calibration cycle in nearly complete form. An initially unexpected event generates a climbing-fiber teaching signal; eligible contextual activity is modified into a timed Purkinje-cell prediction; that prediction produces an anticipatory protective response and inhibits the expected error; and omission of the predicted event generates an opposing signal that trains extinction. Loss, error, plasticity, and behavior are successive views of the same circuit learning to place an action at the precise point in time when it will be needed. Inhibiting the inferior olive disrupts eyeblink learning (Figure).

Saccade and smooth-pursuit learning

Adaptation of saccades and smooth pursuit makes the cerebellar transduction chain visible almost one trial at a time. Saccades are too rapid for visual feedback to correct them during execution, so their amplitude and direction must be calibrated from the error observed after the eye lands. In laboratory adaptation, the target is displaced during the saccade, creating a postsaccadic visual error without altering the command that initiated the movement. Repeated errors gradually change subsequent saccades in the appropriate direction. Smooth-pursuit learning uses an analogous manipulation: a target repeatedly changes velocity or direction at a predictable time, and the eyes gradually begin to generate the required change before the visual instruction occurs 8, 23. A smooth-pursuit experiment separates learning from its expression (Figure) 109. The study measures acquisition and retention of pursuit learning (Figure).

Recordings from the monkey oculomotor vermis have followed the saccadic update through its successive representations. The direction of postsaccadic error determines the probability that a Purkinje cell emits a complex spike, whereas error magnitude alters the temporal distribution of those spikes across the population 8. When a complex spike occurs, the same Purkinje cell shows a depression of its simple-spike response on the next trial. The resulting behavioral change is not an arbitrary reaction to the exact error vector: it is constrained to the correction axis associated with that cell’s preferred complex-spike error direction 8. The olivocerebellar map therefore routes each visual error to a microzone whose output is anatomically aligned with the correction required to reduce it.

Smooth-pursuit learning reveals the same chain with especially fine temporal resolution. A complex spike following an instructive target motion is associated with a precisely timed depression of simple-spike firing on the next trial and with a corresponding learned change in eye velocity 24. The teaching event is also graded: longer-duration complex spikes predict larger trial-to-trial simple-spike depression and stronger behavioral learning 25. Changes in complex-spike probability and duration track changes in the effectiveness of the visual instruction, allowing the climbing-fiber pathway to regulate both whether an update occurs and how large that update should be 26.

With repeated trials, these local updates accumulate into an anticipatory pursuit command. Purkinje cells in the floccular complex acquire learned simple-spike responses that are timed to the expected target change, and many develop on approximately the same timescale as the behavioral adaptation 27. Learning-related activity also appears in the smooth-eye-movement region of the frontal eye fields, although individual cortical neurons express it more episodically than Purkinje cells 23. The learned movement is therefore generated by a distributed cerebro-cerebellar system, but the cerebellar population provides a comparatively stable, precisely timed calibration signal within that system. An experiment varies visual instructions during smooth pursuit (Figure). Pursuit learning is accompanied by changing Purkinje-cell activity (Figure).

Saccade and pursuit learning thus supply a direct experimental demonstration that loss, error, and plasticity are successive views of one update. The visual displacement is the behavioral loss; its climbing-fiber representation selects the responsible microzone and grades the strength of instruction; the complex spike predicts a change in that cell’s simple-spike output; and the altered output produces a directionally appropriate correction on the next movement. Across repetitions, a series of delayed visual errors is converted into a feedforward command that anticipates the perturbation before vision could correct it.

Reaching adaptation

Reaching adaptation extends the same calibration loop to a multi-joint limb, and it is where the behavioral logic is best characterized while parts of the cellular chain remain inferred. Two perturbations dominate the literature. A visuomotor rotation (or displaced cursor) breaks the mapping from hand motion to seen consequence; a force field breaks the mapping from motor command to limb dynamics. Both produce gradual, trial-by-trial change in the feedforward command and characteristic aftereffects when the perturbation is removed, and both are impaired by cerebellar degeneration 28. Lesion–symptom mapping further suggests that the two are not served by one undifferentiated controller: impairment in force-field adaptation correlates with degeneration of intermediate and lateral anterior lobe (lobules I–V), whereas visuomotor impairment correlates with intermediate posterior lobe (lobules VI–X), and success in the two tasks can be statistically independent within the same patient 28, 29. This is what a modular predictive calibrator should look like: separate microzone populations calibrating separate forward models over the same arm.

The teaching signal in this domain is a sensory prediction error rather than the online correction it provokes. Tseng and colleagues dissociated the two by comparing "shooting" movements, which preclude within-movement correction, against "pointing" movements, which permit it; sensory error was present in both. Cerebellar patients were impaired in adaptation regardless, and their poor online corrections did not predict the size of the adaptation deficit, implying that the mismatch between predicted and observed sensory consequence, not the corrective motor output, drives the update 30. This dissociation recurs at the level of clinical deficit: cerebellar patients retain substantial online feedback correction of force perturbations while being profoundly impaired at trial-to-trial error-driven learning 31, 32. The controller survives; the calibrator does not. A reaching experiment compares visual and memory-guided conditions (Figure) 110. The experiment measures changes in reaching direction (Figure).

Isolating that signal behaviorally reveals a loss function that is remarkably indifferent to the task. With task-irrelevant clamped feedback, the cursor follows a fixed angular offset independent of hand direction, and participants are told to ignore it; they nevertheless drift steadily away from the clamp, adapting to a sensory prediction error in the complete absence of task success or failure 33. The update is also bounded rather than proportional: trial-to-trial adaptive corrections scale with error size only for errors below roughly 44–6∘6^\circ, saturating thereafter, and learning functions converge to a similar asymptote across a wide range of error magnitudes 34. Both features fit a supervised calibrator with a fixed, modest gain on an internally defined prediction error, and they explain why explicit re-aiming can flexibly cancel a large rotation while implicit recalibration continues to accumulate underneath it 35, 36.

Rodent work has begun to supply the missing implementation-level chain. In mice, a Purkinje-cell population response that scales inversely with reach velocity identifies the cerebellar cortex as a site linking a within-reach kinematic predictor to anticipatory control; repeated closed-loop optogenetic stimulation of pontocerebellar mossy fibers then acts as a learnable perturbation. When the stimulation was locked to a fixed reach position, both neural and behavioral readouts adapted and showed aftereffects on its removal, whereas position-randomized stimulation produced partial adaptation but no opposing aftereffect 37. This is the predictive-calibration signature in its cleanest form: the circuit learns a correction indexed to a predictable context, and an unpredictable perturbation cannot be absorbed into the forward model. Complementary recordings show the error limb behaving as expected during rapid limb-skill adjustment, with reciprocally modulated parasagittal bands whose complex spiking encodes the sign and magnitude of an imposed perturbation 38.

The output side shows how the learned correction reaches the rest of the motor system. Reversibly blocking cerebellar output in monkeys reaching against a velocity-dependent force field impaired adaptation, as in cerebellar patients, and did so through changes in pre-movement activity: the cortical preparatory state rotated, its dimensionality rose, and generalization across targets degraded at both neural and behavioral levels. A model reproduced these effects by showing that low-dimensional, cerebellar-like feedback compresses the cortical manifold and thereby improves generalization 39. Cerebellar calibration is therefore expressed not only as a corrective signal during movement but as a constraint on how cortex prepares the next one.

Finally, the baseline deficit clarifies what forward model is being calibrated. Reaching ataxia is far worse for multi-joint than single-joint movements, and the classical account attributes this to a failure to predict and compensate for interaction torques—the inertial, centripetal, and Coriolis torques a moving segment imposes on its neighbors 40, 41. Recent work sharpens the picture: initial-direction errors and trajectory curvature are worst when reaches impose tight inter-joint timing requirements and when interaction torques assist the intended movement, exactly the conditions requiring an accurate anticipatory model of limb dynamics rather than more muscle torque 42. Reaching thus displays the full arc: a standing forward model of body dynamics whose failure produces dysmetria, a sensory prediction error that recalibrates that model with a bounded, largely automatic gain, and a cerebellar output that shapes both the ongoing movement and the cortical preparation of the next one.

Locomotor adaptation

Locomotor adaptation extends the same loop to a continuous, rhythmic, whole-body task, and it is the case that most clearly separates a preserved controller from a lost calibrator. The canonical paradigm is the split-belt treadmill, on which two independently driven belts move the legs at different speeds. Walking under this perturbation decomposes into two processes: immediate reactive adjustments of parameters such as stride length and stance time, and slower feedforward adaptation of step length, double-support time, and interlimb timing 43, 44. The interlimb parameters adapt gradually and produce aftereffects when the belts are tied again, the standard signature of predictive learning and storage; spatial and temporal components can also be dissociated experimentally and adapt at different rates 44. Because reactive and predictive changes occur within the same task, the paradigm directly asks which the cerebellum supplies: cerebellar damage largely preserves reactive feedback-driven adjustments but substantially disrupts the slower predictive adaptations and their aftereffects 43. As in reaching, the immediate response to the perturbation survives while its conversion into an anticipatory gait pattern is selectively impaired. A 2025 computational model addresses split-belt walking (Figure) 111. The model produces gradual simulated gait adaptation (Figure). A human study examines transfer after split-belt walking (Figure) 113. The study tests transfer of speed recalibration (Figure).

Noninvasive physiology provides convergent, although not completely consistent, evidence that the cerebellum regulates the rate of locomotor recalibration. In the original split-belt stimulation experiment, anodal cerebellar tDCS accelerated adaptation whereas cathodal stimulation slowed it, without changing de-adaptation; importantly, the effect was selective for spatial rather than temporal components of gait 45. A separate TMS study found that split-belt learning reduced cerebellar-brain inhibition, and that the magnitude of this reduction strongly correlated with the amount of adaptation across individuals 46. Structural differences in the input pathway point in the same direction: diffusion-MRI measures in the inferior cerebellar peduncle, which carries major spinocerebellar afferents into the cerebellum, predict individual differences in locomotor adaptation, whereas comparable measures in the superior cerebellar peduncle and corticospinal tract do not show the same relationship 47. The stimulation result itself is not fully robust, however: a later randomized trial of repeated anodal cerebellar tDCS found no enhancement of split-belt adaptation, although stimulation altered some measures of de-adaptation and maintenance 48. Thus, locomotor learning covaries with cerebellar physiological and anatomical state and can be shifted under some stimulation protocols.

Animal work supplies circuit localization that human studies cannot. Mice adapt to split-belt walking in a strikingly human-like manner: learning is concentrated in measures of interlimb coordination, spatial and temporal components adapt at different rates, and the learned pattern is context-dependent 49. Large cerebral-cortical lesions leave this adaptation largely intact, whereas disrupting the intermediate cerebellum abolishes it; cell-type-specific chemogenetic experiments further dissociate the circuits supporting spatial and temporal learning, with paravermal Purkinje cells projecting to the interposed nucleus required for normal spatial adaptation 49. A complementary 2026 paradigm, LocoReach, examined acquisition of a more complex learned stepping pattern: mice learned to place each paw onto successive treadmill rungs, progressively reducing errors while increasing stride length and swing velocity. Purkinje cells and molecular-layer interneurons in lobule simplex became strongly modulated around learned swing–stance events, and optogenetic disruption of the same region shortened swing duration, placing cerebellar cortical activity directly within the timing of the acquired locomotor pattern 50.

Earlier cat experiments supplied a molecular link. In decerebrate cats, accelerating the belt beneath one forelimb initially disrupted step-cycle and bisupport timing, but repeated exposure restored stable coordination; blocking nitric-oxide synthesis or scavenging nitric oxide locally in cerebellar lobule V abolished this adaptation while sparing ordinary unperturbed locomotion 51. Because nitric oxide participates in several forms of cerebellar synaptic plasticity, this implicated local cerebellar plasticity in the behavioral update 51. The species comparison requires caution, however. Later prolonged split-belt experiments in intact and spinal cats did not reproduce the progressive symmetry restoration and robust aftereffects characteristic of human split-belt adaptation, indicating that not every asymmetric-treadmill response in quadrupeds is homologous to the human paradigm 52. The mouse split-belt preparation therefore provides the cleaner cross-species analogue, while the older cat work remains valuable for localizing cerebellar error signaling and plasticity.

The teaching signal itself is still less completely specified here than in eyeblink or pursuit learning. The mossy-fiber input is well suited to constructing the necessary locomotor state estimate: dorsal spinocerebellar neurons integrate muscle, joint, and cutaneous afference, and their population activity represents global hindlimb variables such as endpoint position, limb-axis length, and orientation rather than simply isolated muscle lengths or joint angles 53, 54, 55. Many dorsal spinocerebellar neurons also respond to movement of the contralateral hindlimb, giving a cerebellar hemisphere bilateral information relevant to estimating interlimb geometry 56. On the teaching side, sudden locomotor perturbations increase climbing-fiber discharge in cerebellar Purkinje cells and synchronously recruit climbing-fiber inputs across sagittally aligned Purkinje-cell populations 57, 58. Computational models make a candidate loss explicit: a cerebellar layer can adapt locomotion by comparing predicted with actual foot-contact timing and feeding the learned timing correction back onto a spinal central-pattern-generator controller 59. But locomotor experiments have not yet followed a particular graded complex-spike event through an identified Purkinje-cell parameter change to a quantitatively predicted correction on the next stride in the way that oculomotor experiments have. Here the behavioral loss and cerebellar dependence are well established, while important links in the cellular transduction chain remain inferred 60.

Locomotion therefore contributes two things to the general picture. It shows predictive calibration operating at whole-body scale, on a periodic behavior whose "trials" are strides rather than discrete movements, while spinal and brainstem circuitry remains capable of generating the underlying rhythm and rapid reactive adjustments 43. And it shows that what gets calibrated is not one scalar gain: spatial and temporal coordinates of interlimb coordination can adapt separately, at different rates, depend on partially dissociable cerebellar circuitry, and leave distinct sensory as well as motor aftereffects 44, 49, 61. The cerebellum is therefore better conceived as calibrating a collection of context-dependent predictive mappings over the evolving gait state than as learning one global correction for "walking".

Speech and sensory cancellation

Speech adaptation extends predictive calibration to a motor system whose most informative consequence is auditory. Producing a vowel requires the vocal tract to generate an expected acoustic output rapidly enough that ordinary auditory feedback, delayed by peripheral and central processing, cannot specify every articulatory command online. In altered-auditory-feedback experiments, the first formant of a spoken vowel can be shifted electronically so that, for example, an intended ‘head’’ sounds closer to ‘hid.’’ When that perturbation is repeated consistently, healthy speakers gradually change their produced formant in the opposite direction and retain an aftereffect when normal feedback is restored, showing that the auditory discrepancy has updated the feedforward speech command 62, 63.

Cerebellar degeneration selectively weakens this conversion from auditory error into future action. Patients exposed repeatedly to a constant formant perturbation adapt substantially less than healthy controls and show little or no reliable washout aftereffect, whether the perturbation is introduced abruptly or gradually 62. Yet when an unpredictable formant shift is inserted on an individual utterance, the same patients can still use auditory feedback to correct the ongoing vocalization. The original study found these reactive corrections to be larger than normal, while a later study found essentially normal feedback gains despite again observing impaired adaptation; across both speech and reaching, cerebellar degeneration consistently impaired feedforward learning while sparing the capacity for immediate feedback correction 62, 63.

The corresponding calibration loop is therefore closely analogous to reaching. An efference copy of the articulatory command predicts the auditory consequence of the utterance; the heard vowel provides the delayed sensory outcome; a mismatch between the two becomes an auditory sensory prediction error; and repeated errors modify the command used on subsequent utterances. Once learned, the correction appears in the early portion of the vowel before an online auditory response could plausibly have generated it 62, 63. This does not mean the cerebellum is completely uninvolved in feedback control: cerebellar stimulation can alter the magnitude and latency of compensatory vocal responses to unpredictable pitch shifts, indicating that cerebello-cortical circuitry can modulate reactive control even though the feedback response itself survives cerebellar degeneration 64. The strongest lesion-level conclusion is narrower: the cerebellum is especially important for turning recurrent auditory errors into updated feedforward predictions.

The same forward model can be used for a second computation: sensory cancellation. If an efference copy predicts not only the state needed to control an action but the sensory input that the action is about to produce, expected reafference can be attenuated while deviations from that prediction remain salient. The classic example is self-generated touch. Identical tactile stimulation feels weaker and less ticklish when produced by one’s own movement than when generated externally, and inserting temporal or spatial discrepancies between the movement and its tactile consequence progressively abolishes this attenuation 65, 66. The critical variable is therefore not merely whether the subject initiated an action but whether the resulting sensation matches its predicted timing and location.

Cerebellar activity is linked to the prediction that produces this attenuation. Early fMRI experiments found reduced somatosensory-cortical responses to self-generated touch together with cerebellar activity consistent with prediction of the movement’s specific tactile consequence; trial-wise coupling between cerebellar and somatosensory activity supported the proposal that this prediction contributes to cortical attenuation 65, 67. A later study combining psychophysics and fMRI strengthened this connection: the greater an individual’s perceptual attenuation of self-generated touch, the stronger the functional coupling between the ipsilateral cerebellum and primary and secondary somatosensory cortices 68. A recent neuroimaging meta-analysis likewise identifies the cerebellum as a recurrent component of the distributed network supporting sensory attenuation 69. A human experiment studies delayed self-generated touch (Figure) 112. The study tracks activity during exposure to delayed touch (Figure).

The principle generalizes across sensory modalities. When healthy subjects trigger a sound themselves, its auditory N1/N100 response is suppressed relative to the same externally generated sound. Patients with focal cerebellar lesions show a strongly attenuated suppression effect, even though the sound is initiated by a simple motor act rather than speech, providing lesion evidence that the cerebellum contributes to a motor-to-auditory forward model 70. Thus, cerebellar sensory prediction is not restricted to predicting proprioception from limb movement: an action can generate a temporally precise prediction in another sensory system, and matching input is treated differently from unexpected input. Cerebellum-like circuits elsewhere in the nervous system implement an especially explicit version of the same computation; in the dorsal cochlear nucleus of mice, mossy-fiber-carried nonauditory signals learn to cancel neural responses to self-generated sounds while preserving responses to external sounds 71.

Speech and sensory cancellation therefore expose two uses of the same learned prediction. In speech adaptation, an auditory residual trains the next motor command until the expected sound is restored; in sensory cancellation, an accurate predicted consequence is used to attenuate the sensory response itself, leaving unexpected residuals relatively salient. The distinction is computationally important: the cerebellar output need not always be a corrective motor command. It can instead be a prediction delivered to another neural system, changing how incoming information is interpreted. Speech consequently forms a useful bridge toward the cerebellum’s proposed non-motor roles: it remains a sensorimotor behavior, but it demonstrates how a learned cerebellar mapping can calibrate the dynamics of cortical sensory processing rather than merely the trajectory of a limb 70, 72.

Is cerebellar learning domain-general? The strongest version of the domain-general hypothesis is not merely that the cerebellum is active during cognition. That much is no longer seriously in doubt. It is that the same basic optimization architecture described throughout this section–high-dimensional contextual input, prediction of a future event, a sparse teaching signal when that prediction fails, and plasticity that changes the next prediction–is reused when the variable being calibrated is not a limb, eye, or vocal tract but a cortical, motivational, social, or affective state. Three claims should therefore be separated. First, the cerebellum participates in non-motor functions and forms loops with association cortex; this is well established. Second, non-motor cerebellar circuits contain predictive, outcome-related, and error-related signals and can causally influence cognition; evidence for this is now substantial. Third, the same local learning algorithm that explains VOR, eyeblink, and sensorimotor adaptation operates unchanged in every cognitive and affective cerebellar territory; this remains an open hypothesis. The relative homogeneity of cerebellar cortical circuitry makes such a "universal cerebellar transform" attractive, but functional heterogeneity across cerebellar regions and major differences between the cortical systems into which they are embedded prevent anatomy alone from establishing algorithmic identity 73, 74, 75.

The anatomy nevertheless makes reuse plausible. Cerebro-cerebellar communication is organized as many partially segregated loops rather than as a diffuse cerebellar broadcast. Widespread sensory, motor, and association cortex projects through the pontine nuclei into the mossy-fiber system, while cortical information can also reach the olivocerebellar teaching system through indirect cerebro-olivary pathways; cerebellar nuclear output then returns through thalamus to motor, premotor, prefrontal, and posterior-parietal territories, often closing loops with cortical regions that themselves provide cerebellar input 76, 77. Granule-cell populations can preserve substantial structure from neocortical dynamics entering through the pons, allowing the cerebellum to receive an evolving copy of cortical state and feed transformed signals back into the same distributed system; this has motivated treating the neocortex and cerebellum as a joint dynamical system rather than as an autonomous cortical controller followed by a motor corrector 77.

Human functional organization mirrors this anatomical breadth. A large NeuroSynth-based analysis pooling task coordinates from more than 44,500 participants recovered cerebellar territories corresponding not only to sensorimotor processing but to dorsal and ventral attention, executive control, mentalizing/default-mode processing, language, and smaller limbic territories, broadly converging with resting-state and other task-based parcellations 78, 79, 80, 81. On a predictive-calibration account, nothing in the local learning problem requires xtx_t to mean arm state” or the output to mean muscle correction.” Mossy-fiber context could instead encode a cortical task state, an abstract cue, a linguistic sequence, another agent’s behavior, or an interoceptive state; the relevant climbing-fiber system could report a task-specific unexpected outcome; and nuclear output could alter the future dynamics of the cortical or subcortical network that generated that state. What changes from module to module would then be the semantics of the inputs, teaching signal, and target circuit, while the computational format—learn an anticipatory mapping that reduces future residual error—could remain similar 74, 75. This is the precise sense in which predictive calibration could be domain-general without requiring one global cerebellar loss function.

Reward learning currently provides some of the strongest evidence that the content supplied to cerebellar learning can extend beyond classical motor error. In mice learning operant and Pavlovian tasks, granule-cell populations encode reward delivery, reward omission, and reward expectation, with some predictive responses emerging over the course of learning 82. The teaching pathway is equally flexible. Climbing-fiber inputs to Purkinje cells develop predictive responses to reward-associated cues and reactive responses to reward outcomes, and recordings across reward-learning paradigms have identified signals related to expected reward, unexpected reward, omission, and outcome surprise 83, 84, 85, 86. Human data now point in the same direction. In a 2026 reinforcement-learning experiment designed without low-level sensorimotor contingencies, cognitive regions spanning Crus I/II encoded reward and model-derived reward-prediction errors; strikingly, these signals were robust when outcome feedback followed the choice rapidly but became undetectable at supra-second delays, unlike corresponding signals in ventral striatum and hippocampus 87. Reward therefore provides a particularly clear demonstration of domain-generality at the level of the teaching variable: the same cerebellar architecture that can be trained by retinal slip, sensory prediction error, or an aversive unconditioned stimulus can also receive learned reward and outcome signals. The temporal constraint is equally revealing–even when the predicted consequence is reward rather than movement error, cerebellar learning appears strongest when that consequence falls within the relatively short predictive horizon characteristic of the system. A human study compares monetary and social feedback (Figure) 114. The study maps brain responses to correct and incorrect outcomes (Figure).

An even cleaner test is to remove action altogether. A July 2026 human fMRI preprint did exactly this using passive visual statistical learning: participants simply viewed sequences whose stimulus-to-stimulus transition probabilities varied, made no choice about the transitions, and reported no explicit knowledge of the regularities afterward. Nevertheless, putative cognitive regions of the cerebellum tracked trial-by-trial prediction errors as the transition structure was learned. Computational modeling fit the cerebellar signal with an incremental delta-rule learner whose expectations changed gradually with recent experience, whereas anterior hippocampal activity was better characterized by a representation of the underlying transition distribution. If replicated, this result is unusually important for the domain-general hypothesis because neither a motor command nor reward is needed to produce a cerebellar learning-like error signal: the quantity being predicted is simply what visual event comes next 88. The result should still be placed one level below the motor case studies in mechanistic confidence; fMRI cannot establish that the measured error is carried by climbing fibers, identify which synapses are modified, or show that a particular complex spike causes a particular parameter update. Other cognitive tasks reveal pieces of that chain at finer resolution. In a mouse evidence-accumulation task, animals integrated a sequence of sensory samples before reporting which side contained more evidence. Inactivation of posterior cerebellar Crus I reduced decision accuracy, Purkinje-cell somatic activity represented accumulated evidence and upcoming choice, and dendritic calcium events—closely associated with climbing-fiber-driven complex spikes—were enhanced following decision errors; importantly, measured orofacial and limb movements could not account for the encoded choice and evidence variables 89. Here, an abstract internal variable is present in the Purkinje output stream, a behaviorally relevant “error” appears in the dendritic teaching compartment, and perturbing the circuit impairs the computation, although the experiment does not yet trace that error through synaptic modification into improved future decisions. Likewise, chemogenetic inhibition of Purkinje cells in lobule VI or Crus I allowed mice to acquire an initial Y-maze rule but selectively impaired reversal learning, while simultaneously reorganizing activity across a distributed diencephalic and neocortical network 90. These experiments move substantially beyond correlational cognitive activation, but they still provide fragments rather than the nearly closed learning loop available for eyeblink or oculomotor adaptation. A 2026 experiment tests cerebellar contributions to decision learning (Figure) 115. Complex-spike responses vary with behavioral state (Figure).

The output side suggests what "cognitive calibration" might physically mean. Cerebellar output does not have to specify an overt movement; through thalamic and other relays it can alter the recurrent dynamics generated by cerebral cortex. In a delayed sensory-discrimination task, preparatory activity encoding an upcoming action was present simultaneously in frontal cortex and cerebellar nuclei seconds before movement. Silencing frontal cortex abolished the cerebellar preparatory signal, but cerebellar-nuclear activity was in turn necessary to maintain the corresponding cortical state; cerebellar output returned through thalamus selectively to the behaviorally relevant cortical territory, completing a recurrent cortico-cerebellar loop 91, 77. Thus, even though the eventual behavior in this experiment was motor, the computational object controlled by the cerebellum was an internally maintained cortical state rather than an ongoing muscle command.

Motor adaptation provides an especially concrete demonstration of the same principle. Blocking cerebellar outflow during force-field learning changed the geometry of motor-cortical preparatory activity, increased its dimensionality, degraded neural and behavioral generalization, and was reproduced by a model in which low-dimensional cerebellar feedback constrains the cortical preparatory manifold 39. The learned product of the cerebellum can therefore be understood not only as a correction added downstream of cortex but as a calibration signal that helps place a recurrent cortical network into an appropriate region of state space before behavior unfolds. This framing generalizes naturally to association cortex: if a cortical network maintains a task state, linguistic context, decision variable, or social model, cerebellar output could improve behavior by stabilizing, advancing, or reshaping that trajectory rather than by directly specifying the behavioral output. A 2025 study tests cerebellar output during motor adaptation (Figure) 116. Cerebellar pathway stimulation alters adaptation (Figure).

Recent experiments and models extend that idea from transient dynamics to learning within cortex itself. Optogenetic activation of climbing fibers in awake mice suppresses experience-dependent potentiation of whisker responses in layer 2/3 of primary somatosensory cortex; the effect depends on SST/VIP interneuron circuitry and a cerebellar-output pathway involving zona incerta and posterior medial thalamus 92. The olivocerebellar teaching system can therefore influence what another brain area learns rather than merely correcting the cerebellum’s own output. A systems-level model makes the stronger cognitive proposal explicit: a feedforward cerebellar network receives the state of a recurrent cortical network, learns task-specific predictions, and feeds them back to steer cortical dynamics; this architecture supports rapid task acquisition and context switching, sustains cortical states in a delayed-association/working-memory task, and can in principle transfer a learned solution into recurrent cortical weights during consolidation 93.

Language and social cognition demonstrate that the candidate target circuits are genuinely domain-specific rather than merely motor areas recruited by difficult tasks. Precision fMRI recently identified four right posterior cerebellar regions that respond reliably to language; one region spanning Crus I/II and lobule VIIb was strongly selective for language relative to a broad battery of non-linguistic tasks, responded during both comprehension and production, scaled with linguistic difficulty, and was tightly coupled to the neocortical language network 94. Social prediction shows a parallel organization: effective-connectivity modeling across four datasets found bidirectional loops between posterior cerebellar Crus regions and the cerebral mentalizing network during prediction of social action sequences 95. These are strong demonstrations that association cerebellum is embedded in computations whose content is linguistic and social, not merely motor. They are not, however, demonstrations of cerebellar learning in the same sense as VOR or eyeblink conditioning. We do not yet know what climbing fibers report to a language microzone, what constitutes a signed “linguistic error,” or which local plasticity changes when a person becomes better at predicting a sentence. Indeed, the inability to observe human inferior-olive teaching signals is identified as one of the central unresolved obstacles to a mechanistic theory of cerebellar cognition 74.

Development adds an important wrinkle to this picture: cerebellar calibration may help construct some non-motor networks rather than merely modulate them after they are mature. Whole-brain developmental tracing in mice shows that long-range cerebellar outputs are established remarkably early. Cerebellar efferents begin reaching major hypothalamic, midbrain, prethalamic, and thalamic targets during embryonic and perinatal development; presynaptic terminals appear around the same period, followed by rapid postnatal expansion and region-specific refinement, with the broad target pattern largely established within the first postnatal week 96. This early access to brain-wide circuitry is notable because the behavioral consequences of cerebellar injury are strongly age-dependent. A review of social-cognitive outcomes reports profound effects after prenatal cerebellar disruption, substantial deficits following childhood injury, but considerably milder and less consistent social deficits after comparable adult cerebellar damage 97. The authors propose that early cerebellar forward-model learning may use prediction errors to help construct internal schemas of the social world; that particular mechanism remains hypothetical, but the developmental gradient itself supports a broader conclusion: cerebellar influence on cognition may include developmental scaffolding, in which predictive output helps shape the cortical and subcortical dynamics that later support mature cognition 97.

The proposed extension to affective and interoceptive calibration is similarly compelling at the systems level but substantially less complete at the learning-rule level. Cerebellar damage can produce the cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome, including deficits in executive control, language and visuospatial organization together with flattening, disinhibition, or other dysregulation of affect 98. Across 80 human neuroimaging studies and 2,761 participants, emotional processing consistently recruited posterior hemispheric and vermal cerebellar territories 99. Animal experiments now show direct control over homeostatic variables as well: cerebellar Purkinje neurons respond to the circulating hormone asprosin, and selective manipulation of this pathway causally changes water drinking without impairing cerebellar motor learning or coordination; separate work identifies deep cerebellar circuitry capable of modulating satiation 100, 101. These findings establish that the variables available to cerebellar circuits include motivational, autonomic, and internal-body-state information 102.

A predictive-calibration interpretation of these findings would say that some cerebellar modules learn the expected trajectory, timing, or gain of an internal response rather than an external movement. An affective module might predict how strongly an autonomic or emotional state should evolve given the current context and then correct responses that are too large, too small, too early, or too late; an interoceptive module might predict the near-future bodily consequence of ingestion, thirst, visceral state, or action and tune downstream hypothalamic, brainstem, or cortical circuitry accordingly. Schmahmann’s description of cerebellar pathology as dysmetria of thought is naturally compatible with this view: just as a damaged motor cerebellum overshoots and undershoots in physical space, damaged association or limbic loops could produce responses whose magnitude, timing, or contextual scaling is poorly calibrated 103, 98, 102. But the analogy should not be mistaken for a demonstrated transduction chain. In affect and interoception, current experiments identify inputs, outputs, activation patterns, and causal behavioral effects far more clearly than they identify the relevant climbing-fiber residual, its eligibility trace, or the parameter update that reduces that residual on the next encounter. "Affective calibration" is therefore a strong systems-level hypothesis, not yet the equivalent of retinal-slip-driven VOR adaptation.

This is where the debate over a universal cerebellar transform ultimately lands. The repeating cerebellar microcircuit suggests a reusable computational primitive, but relative anatomical uniformity does not require computational identity: molecular and physiological differences exist across cerebellar territories, cortical inputs converge differently across modules, and different target networks have radically different intrinsic dynamics 73, 74. One recent alternative is therefore to look for common constraints rather than one literal universal function: cerebellar computations tend to be predictive rather than purely reactive, especially useful over relatively short temporal horizons, and suited to continuously varying quantities such as position, time, probability, or evolving neural state 104.

Synthesis

Motor paradigms expose essentially the entire transduction chain of cerebellar learning: a well-defined behavioral loss generates a climbing-fiber teaching signal, that signal acts on eligible cerebellar states, plasticity changes Purkinje/nuclear output, and the next movement contains an anticipatory correction. Reward and decision tasks show that both the contextual basis and the teaching pathway can encode abstract task variables, while human reward learning shows that the same error-like computations retain the cerebellum’s characteristic temporal constraints. Passive statistical learning now provides preliminary evidence that a cerebellar prediction-error computation can operate even when there is no action to calibrate at all. Cerebro-cerebellar experiments further show that the learned output can reshape or stabilize the dynamics of the recurrent networks with which the cerebellum is coupled, and developmental evidence raises the possibility that this interaction helps construct those networks during sensitive periods. Language, social cognition, affect, and interoception establish still broader input/output territories, but their local losses, climbing-fiber teachers, and plasticity rules remain largely the missing middle 74, 105, 75, 88. The safest unifying claim is that evolution has repeatedly embedded a high-capacity, temporally precise, error-trainable predictive module inside different control loops, allowing the same broad optimization format to calibrate whatever variable that loop needs to keep predictable. In movement we can watch nearly every step of that optimization happen; outside movement, the evidence increasingly suggests the same motif, while the decisive experiments that close the loss () error () plasticity () improved prediction loop are only beginning to arrive.
